{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A man in his 60s has longstanding asthma, nasal polyps, sinus disease and previous eosinophilia up to 3.8×10^9/L. ANCA was negative and earlier biopsies did not show vasculitis. A clinical diagnosis of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis had been made. Mepolizumab controlled symptoms for five years; he stopped it two years ago.
Asthma and sinus symptoms returned over the past year. He developed right facial pain seven months ago, steroid-responsive bilateral facial weakness five months ago and painful right visual loss three months ago. Vision improved after prednisone and doxycycline, without establishing which intervention explained it.
Following a prednisone reduction from 30 to 20 mg, right V2 pain and sensory loss persisted. An outside MRI reading emphasised small-vessel and sinus changes; institutional review describes multifocal dural enhancement. Later symptoms, cardiac tests and treatment response are not supplied.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the evolving neurological problem and compare up to three explanations. Explain how the historical disease label, negative tests, steroid response and revised imaging should influence a provisional assessment and urgent further review. Use only the information supplied at this decision point. Distinguish observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent results, doses, probabilities or events. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "**Provisional Assessment and Differential**

Observed facts: multifocal dural enhancement on institutional MRI; steroid-responsive bilateral facial weakness; painful right visual loss with partial recovery; persistent right V2 pain and sensory loss after prednisone reduction; prior eosinophilia to 3.8×10⁹/L; ANCA-negative; no biopsy-confirmed vasculitis; symptom recurrence after mepolizumab cessation.

Three explanations to weigh:

**EGPA relapse with neurological involvement.** The clinical label was established without histological confirmation of vasculitis and with negative ANCA. Mepolizumab dependence and symptom recurrence after withdrawal support an eosinophil-driven process. Multifocal dural enhancement may reflect eosinophilic infiltration or small-vessel vasculitis. However, the absence of confirmed vasculitis on prior biopsies means the label remains provisional.

**Idiopathic or eosinophilic hypertrophic pachymeningitis.** Multifocal dural enhancement is the dominant imaging finding. This pattern can occur in EGPA but also as a distinct entity. Steroid responsiveness is consistent but non-specific.

**Infectious dural/sinus process.** Doxycycline was co-administered with prednisone; the contribution of each to visual recovery is unestablished. Chronic sinus disease is a risk factor, though bilateral facial weakness and multifocal dural involvement are atypical for simple infection.

**Influence on provisional assessment:** The negative ANCA and absent vasculitis on prior biopsy weaken the EGPA label but do not exclude it. The steroid response confirms an inflammatory or immune-mediated process but does not distinguish among the three. The revised imaging (multifocal dural enhancement) shifts the focus from small-vessel disease to a dural-based process, which may represent a different pathophysiology than originally assumed.
